boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's siege and capture of Gaëta (4 March to 18 July 1806 by Bodart) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1806 group: the French investment and blockade of the fortress from February, the bombardment attempts begun in March, the siege works, the fire opened on 7 July, the capitulation of 18 July and the French entry on the 19th. The first investment by Reynier's troops on the march into the kingdom, Campo Tenese (B370c), Maida (B370d), the siege of Scilla and the risings in Calabria are context. Side A is the French. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) 3,000 men during the blockade and 12,000 men toward the end of the siege, with 94 guns, under Marshal Masséna, and side B (the Neapolitan garrison) originally 4,000 men, always supplied with provisions through the effective support of Rear-Admiral Sidney Smith's English squadron and brought to 7,000 men by successive reinforcements, under Captain-General Prince of Hesse-Philippsthal. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. His 3,000 for the blockade is Koch's figure for the troops the blockade required, and his 12,000 at the end Koch's statement that the troops employed never exceeded 12,000, beside a printed total of 12,016 in Koch's state of the siege troops (claim koch-side-a); Colletta has fourteen thousand besiegers (claim colletta-side-a). His 94 guns are not in the passages read: Koch's siege batteries held 90 pieces, with a mobile battery of 4 twelve-pounders and 2 six-inch howitzers to be added, which make 94 without the howitzers and 96 with them (our arithmetic). His 7,000 for the garrison at the end is Koch's in his reflections and Colletta's for 7 July (claims koch-side-b and colletta-side-b); his original 4,000 is not in the passages read, where Koch's composition of the garrison before the siege makes fewer than 6,000 men. The figures span the blockade and the siege, so the phase is unresolved. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'the French (during the blockade 3,000 men, toward the end of the siege 12,000 men strong with 94 guns) under Marshal Masséna, after five months' investment and more than four months' siege, force the Neapolitan garrison (originally 4,000 men, through the effective support of the English squadron of Rear-Admiral Sidney Smith always supplied with provisions, and brought to 7,000 men by successive reinforcements) under Captain-General Prince of Hesse-Philippsthal to capitulate'. 'Gen.-Kpt.' is General-Kapitän, 'C.-A.' Contre-Admiral and 'Pz.' Prinz in Bodart's list of abbreviations.

claims.value: Side A (French), its own account in Koch: with most of the 1st corps at Naples, the blockade of Gaëte required 3,000 men; the army's organisation had detached troops before Gaëte to form its blockade until the siege could be undertaken (OCR); when General Lacour broke off the first talks his brigade did not exceed 2,400 men and lacked siege artillery. Until the middle of May the siege brigade was reinforced only by 5 companies of artillery, a detachment of black pioneers, a company of miners, 2 of sappers, the 10e de ligne, a Corsican battalion and a company of dragoons, bringing it to 4,000 men; from 17 May, when General of Division Gardanne took command of the siege troops, until 6 July successive reinforcements brought it to about twelve thousand men of all arms. At the time of the night of the 5th to the 6th the siege corps had 8,500 men of all arms before the place, 800 on the Garigliano and 900 in the posts from the camp to Terracina. Koch's state of the troops employed at the blockade and siege (pièce justificative n° IX) prints artillery 747, engineers 238, infantry 7,836, cavalry 772, foreign infantry 1,954 and foreign cavalry (the 1er régiment napolitain) 469, a total of 12,016, and notes that the troops employed in the attacks and the posts round the camp never exceeded 12,000 men. The siege batteries held 90 pieces, with a mobile battery of 4 twelve-pounders and 2 six-inch howitzers. In his reflections Koch writes that for more than four months 3,000 men held out alone against 6,000, and that only in the last two months of the siege were the troops brought to double the garrison.
claims.rationale: Side A's history, read from the page images except the blockade's first detachment (OCR; its units are not restated). Koch follows the force as it grew: 3,000 for the blockade, 2,400 in Lacour's brigade, 4,000 by mid-May and about twelve thousand by 6 July. His three July figures make 10,200 (our arithmetic), below the twelve thousand of p. 223; the state of pièce n° IX counts the troops employed at the blockade and siege, not a single day's strength, and its section totals make 12,016 (our arithmetic), as printed. For his 3,000 against 6,000 Koch refers to pièce justificative n° XI, which in the parent OCR is a note on King Joseph's guard (checked; not cited), so the passages read do not explain the reference. The blockade force was the detachment the army's organisation made, and the build-up from May followed the generals' requests and the measures the marshal had the king take (claim side-a-command); the claim mixes inherited and commander-made parts and is tagged unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'most of the 1st corps was at Naples, where no fewer than 6,000 men of garrison were needed; the blockade of Gaëte required 3,000' (p. 187); 'the army therefore received (see pièces justificatives, n° III) a new organisation'; '[troops] were detached before Gaëte, of which they formed the blockade, until the siege could be undertaken' (OCR); 'this restriction piqued General Lacour, and despite the weakness of his brigade, which did not exceed 2,400 men, and his lack of siege artillery, he would yield nothing' (p. 196); 'until the middle of the month of May the siege brigade had been reinforced only by 5 companies of artillery, a detachment of black pioneers, a company of miners, 2 of sappers, the 10th of the line, a Corsican battalion and a company of dragoons, which brought its total strength to 4,000 men. On the 17th General of Division Gardanne came to take command of the siege troops. From that moment until 6 July the troops received successive reinforcements which brought their number to about twelve thousand men of all arms' (p. 223); 'night of the 5th to the 6th'; 'the siege corps consisted at that time of 8,500 men of all arms before the place, 800 on the Garigliano and 900 spread among the various posts from the camp to Terracina' (p. 233); 'state of the troops employed at the blockade and siege of Gaete'; 'N. B. — the general total of the troops employed either in the attacks or in the posts around the siege camp never exceeded 12,000 men' (p. 419); 'in all 90 pieces, to which must be added 4 twelve-pounders and 2 six-inch howitzers, forming a mobile battery' (p. 236); 'for more than four months 3,000 men, worn out with fatigue and badly fed, hold out alone against 6,000 men abundantly provided with everything ... for it was only in the last two months of the siege that the number of troops was brought to double that of the garrison' (p. 250).

claims.value: Side A in Colletta: the king's council decided to hasten the surrender of Gaeta so as to use in the rebel provinces the fourteen thousand soldiers besieging the fortress; on the 6th [July] all the batteries were armed with eighty heavy guns and mortars; on 7 July the besieged were about seven thousand, half the besiegers; twelve Neapolitan boats fought on the French side against the Sicilian and English ships.
claims.rationale: Side A's strength in the Neapolitan history, read from the page images. Colletta's fourteen thousand is above Koch's 12,016 for all the troops employed and his ceiling of 12,000 (claim koch-side-a) and Bodart's 12,000; his eighty heavy guns and mortars are below Koch's 90 pieces in the siege batteries. The passages read do not say whether his fourteen thousand counts the posts away from the camp. The council's decision, taken above the siege command, set the effort, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'the state of the army had come to such a pass that in the king's council it was examined whether the troops should now be gathered in a strong place of the Abruzzi to await help from France or from time'; 'the king inclining to the weaker course, Saliceti to the stronger, it was decided that, doubling the means and toils of war, the surrender of Gaeta should be hastened, so as to use in the rebel provinces fourteen thousand soldiers, besiegers of that fortress, and that Marshal Massena should be sent there at once, whose fame and talent would bring help and spirit to his own and harm and dismay to the enemy' (p. 28); 'several times the Sicilian and English ships, coming to battle, were driven off with shame and loss, twelve Neapolitan boats fighting on the French side'; 'on the first of July, having begun the [transport of the artillery]' (p. 29); 'on the 6th, all the batteries armed with eighty cannon of heavy calibre and mortars' (p. 30); 'on the day of the first fire, 7 July, the besieged amounted to about seven thousand, half the besiegers' (p. 30).

claims.value: Side B in Koch: the garrison consisted of 2 battalions of the regiment of the presidi (galley convicts), 2 of the Principe Real regiment, 2 of the Queen Carolina regiment, a battalion of Apulian chasseurs, 2 free corps (insurgent bandits), a small detachment of cavalry, 2 companies of light artillery and a detachment of coast artillery, in all fewer than 6,000 men, enough for an active defence had it been better composed, but made up only of convicts or recruits. On the 10th and 11th [April] the place was resupplied by sea and received 74 gunners or sappers, 200 infantry and 4 long-range howitzers; from the 4th to the 7th [May] the English squadron, of 10 warships, 2 ships of the line, 3 frigates, 1 brig and 10 transports, lay before Gaëte and resupplied it, and Sidney Smith gave the governor 3 thirty-pounders and 2,000 round shot of that calibre. Early in July (the day is heavily inked on the page image) an English squadron escorted transports that landed 2 battalions of the Val di Mezzara regiment and a body of Camisoti, about 1,500 men in all; at the time of the night of the 5th to the 6th the garrison was about 6,200 men by the deserters' report. When the French batteries were armed the place had 103 heavy pieces, 16 mortars and 7 stone mortars in battery against the attacks and, besides some large ships, about fifty gunboats, bomb-vessels and small craft; on 7 July the enemy fleet was 3 ships of the line, 4 frigates, 20 launches and 3 bomb-vessels. In his reflections Koch gives the place 7,000 men of garrison for 3 to 4,000 inhabitants.
claims.rationale: Side A's history on side B, read from the page images; second-hand, the July strength by deserters' report. Koch's composition of fewer than 6,000 is not dated in the passage read; it follows his reconnaissance of the place, before the siege. His figures run from fewer than 6,000 through about 6,200 in early July to 7,000 in his reflections, against Bodart's original 4,000 brought to 7,000 (claim bodart-strength). The first figure of the number of Camisoti is heavily inked on the page image and is not restated; the landing stands in Koch's journal of early July, and its day is also heavily inked and is not restated. The garrison was the force the court of Palermo and the English squadron put and kept in the place, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'the garrison of the place consisted of 2 battalions of the regiment of the presidi (galley convicts), 2 of the Principe Real regiment, 2 of the Queen Carolina regiment, a battalion of the chasseurs of Apulia, 2 free corps (insurgent bandits), a small detachment of cavalry, 2 companies of light artillery, a detachment of coast artillery, the whole forming fewer than 6,000 men' (p. 202); '[the strength] of this garrison would have been more than enough to dispute the approaches and adopt the system of active defence had it been better composed; but there were only convicts or recruits in it' (p. 203); 'night of the 6th to the 7th April'; 'on the 10th and the 11th the place is resupplied by sea and receives a reinforcement of 74 gunners or sappers, 200 infantrymen and 4 long-range howitzers' (p. 212); 'nevertheless, in the night of the 1st to the 2nd May'; 'from the 4th to the 7th the English squadron, composed of 10 warships, 2 ships of the line, 3 frigates, 1 brig and 10 transports, anchors before Gaëte, which it resupplies, and Sidney Smith makes the governor a present of 3 thirty-pounders and 2,000 round shot of that calibre' (p. 218); 'the same day an English squadron also appears before the place, escorting transports which land there 2 battalions of the regiment of Val di Mezzara and ... Camisoti, forming in all about 1,500 men' (p. 231); 'the strength of the garrison came, by the report of the deserters, to about 6,200 men' (p. 233); 'at that time the place had in battery, on the land front as on the sea front, 103 heavy pieces, 16 mortars and 7 stone mortars opposed to our attacks. It had at its disposal besides, apart from some large ships, about fifty gunboats, bomb-vessels and other small craft'; 'the enemy fleet, composed of 3 ships of the line, 4 frigates, 20 launches and 3 bomb-vessels' (p. 236); 'what was it to do against a place of 3 to 4,000 souls which had 7,000 men of garrison?' (p. 249).

claims.value: Side B in Colletta: Gaeta, strengthened with new garrisons, threatened the French camp (OCR); in the fortress the number of soldiers grew, war supplies and food were abundant, tired or sick troops were exchanged for new ones and retreat onto the ships was sure (OCR). On 7 July the besieged were about seven thousand, half the besiegers, and four English ships of the line, six frigates, thirty gunboats or bomb-vessels and some transports cruised round the fortress or lay in the port; the besieged answered the opening of the French fire with more shots, having more abundant artillery. At the surrender the prisoners were three thousand four hundred, and some hundreds more stayed in the hospitals on the same terms; others escaped free by sea, and others went over secretly to the victor. The English and Sicilians besieging the French in the fort of Scilla were under orders to go to Gaeta, once the fort fell, to increase its garrison (OCR).
claims.rationale: Side B's strength in the Neapolitan history, read from the page images except the passages marked OCR. Colletta's about seven thousand on 7 July agrees with Bodart's 7,000 and Koch's 7,000 in his reflections and is above Koch's 6,200 by deserters' report for the same days (claim koch-side-b). His ships are more than Koch's enemy fleet of 7 July, 3 ships of the line and 4 frigates. The passages read give no garrison strength at the surrender beside his prisoners. claims.value: Side A's command and decisions. Koch: the marshal entrusted the preparatory works of attack to Generals Dedon and Vallongue and the command of the troops to General Lacour (OCR). Lacour, persuaded that the prince would hand over the place under the capitulation already concluded (that of Capua, OCR), refused the prince's condition of no French post in the faubourg, and the talks broke off. Lacour hoped, through intelligence he had created in the place, to master it by a simple bombardment, while Vallongue asked for the same number of troops as the engineers and about twenty guns and wanted the means to push the siege if the bombardment failed; the marshal judged it prudent to suspend operations until resources were obtained from outside, but Joseph strongly approved Lacour's plan and it was decided to carry it out (OCR); the marshal remarked that the planned fire seemed to him insufficient (OCR); a new attempt was ordered notwithstanding the representations of the marshal and of the engineer and artillery generals (OCR); in Koch's reflections the king imposed his will on the marshal and the generals. When the English squadron reached Messina the marshal armed the coasts with the siege artillery, had Lacour send back to Naples the pieces not yet in battery and, to conform to the king's intentions, told him to confine himself to improving the works and fortifying himself on the coast (OCR). General of Division Gardanne took command of the siege troops on 17 May; on 18 May the marshal visited the trenches with the engineer and artillery generals and the commander of the siege troops; the marshal decided the king to reduce Gaëte at any cost, and Gardanne was ordered to hasten the batteries (OCR). Told that all would be ready to open fire within 8 days, the marshal decided the king to visit the siege camp with him; the king returned at once to Naples, and from then on the marshal followed the siege and set up his headquarters at Castellone. He made a last summons before opening fire; the batteries opened on 7 July at the king's signal; he rejected General Dedon's proposal to reduce the fire for fear of running out of powder and bombs, and renewed his summons through General Donzelot (OCR). For the assault the columns were to be led by Generals Donzelot and Valentin, with General Lamarque's column to join Donzelot and General Caracciolo, commanding the Neapolitan troops at the siege, in reserve under General Gardanne (OCR); when the place offered terms the marshal sent General Franceschi into it with full powers (OCR), and Franceschi signed the capitulation in the marshal's name, approved by the marshal. Pièce n° IX lists General Dulauloy commanding the artillery and Campredon and Vallongue as engineer generals. Colletta: in the king's council, the king inclining to the weaker course and Saliceti to the stronger, it was decided to hasten the surrender of Gaeta and to send Marshal Massena there at once.

claims.value: Side B's command. Colletta: the regency agreed to hand the fortresses over to the enemy, against King Ferdinand's command never to cede them, and the Prince of Philipstadt, who held the government of Gaeta, answered that he disobeyed its command, by higher commands and the honour of war (OCR). Koch: the Prince of Hesse, governor, sent back the body of squadron leader Lamy, killed by the garrison's fire when presenting himself under flag of truce, with his regrets; at the interview, to which he sent his first aide-de-camp, an armistice was agreed until new instructions came from the court of Palermo, and he accepted the line of investment on condition that the French put no post in the faubourg; when Lacour refused, the talks broke off, he had the house where Lacour lodged bombarded and prepared a vigorous defence (OCR for the last two words); he sent Fra Diavolo and his band out of the place to land at the mouth of the Garigliano and harass the French rear (OCR); he confined himself to the simple defence of the works and risked only the two sorties of 25 April and 15 May; encouraged by Sidney Smith's help, he kept up a very lively fire from ramparts and gunboats, threw fire-balls at night and attempted a small landing toward Fondi, which was repulsed. Deserters reported him mortally wounded while visiting the Brèche bastion; he had been carried dying on board an English ship, which was kept from the French, and Colonel Hotz, who replaced him, put the marshal's letter to a council of war whose majority was for holding out longer (OCR); Hotz, who knew the results of the landing at Santa Eufemia and that the Calabrian insurrection was confined to the Basilicata, was shaken by the English offer to carry the garrison to Palermo but did not accept it (OCR); the capitulation was negotiated under the full powers of Colonel François Hotz, commandant of the place and governor ad interim, and ratified by him. Colletta: Philipstadt's firm mind and valour, supreme in the fortress, added strength to the garrison (OCR); he was wounded in the head; Colonel Storz, who took his place after his mortal wound, brave and resolved on war himself, had the weak authority of a second and commanded by councils, and the besieged asked for terms, as they would certainly not have done had Philipstadt been in the fortress.
claims.rationale: Side B's command as the accounts give it (page images except the passages marked OCR). Koch judges that the governor perhaps did not draw from his position all the advantage possible and that ships gathered in the coves on both sides of the isthmus would have taken the besiegers in flank and rear (OCR). claims.value: Bodart records that side A (French) under Masséna forced the Neapolitan garrison to capitulate after five months' investment and more than four months' siege, dating the siege from 4 March to 18 July 1806; the garrison was allowed to march out with all the honours of war and, against the obligation not to serve against France or its allies for a year, was carried by ship to Sicily, and the French found 171 guns. Koch: the articles of capitulation, requested by the place after a siege of 165 days and the opening of two breaches, were signed on 18 July 1806 at 11 in the evening; in consideration of its valiant defence they let the garrison embark with arms and baggage on the express condition that its corps not serve against France or its allies or King Joseph Napoleon for a year and a day, granted it 8 field pieces and ten days' victuals, and required the rest of the artillery and all the magazines to be handed over. The French entered Gaëte on the 19th at 4 in the morning, the columns of Generals Donzelot and Valentin entering by the breaches, and found 140 cannon, 21 mortars, 3 stone mortars, 7 howitzers, 1,850 muskets, 450 pikes or scythes, 2,225 kilograms of powder and 70,000 cartridges; the siege ended after 5 months of blockade, 4 of open trench and 11 days of continuous fire. The garrison had the honours of war and embarked to be taken to Palermo, and several of its officers and soldiers took service in King Joseph's troops (OCR). Colletta: Gaeta surrendered on the 18th of July; at the first light of the 18th the French formed in column and simulated the movement that precedes mounting the breach, and the besieged asked for terms; it was agreed the same day to give Gaeta up to the French and embark the garrison for Sicily after an oath not to fight against France and its allies for a year and a day.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome (side A won), read from Bodart's entry, with the other accounts' ending (page images except the passage marked OCR). The accounts agree on the capitulation of 18 July; Bodart's year against Koch's and Colletta's year and a day is a difference in the reported terms. Koch's guns found make 171 (our arithmetic: 140, 21, 3 and 7), Bodart's figure. Bodart's first date is the evening on which Koch has the first mortar battery begun (p. 205); the passages read do not say what Bodart's date marks, and Koch and Colletta date the investment from February (claims side-a-command and posture). The articles are printed by Koch in French, 'translated from the Italian original'. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength, and '1806 4/3-18/7. siege and capture of Gaëta'; 'the garrison was allowed to march out with all the honours of war and, against the obligation not to serve against France or its allies for a year, was carried by ship to Sicily. The French found 171 guns'; Koch, 'on the evening of 4 March, then, as had been resolved, mortar battery no. 1 is begun in the garden of the Augustinians or Recollects, covered from the place by the enclosure walls' (p. 205); 'articles of the capitulation requested by the place of Gaete after a siege of 165 days and the opening of two breaches'; 'in consideration of the valiant defence of the garrison of Gaëte, it is permitted to embark with arms and baggage on the express condition that the corps composing it may not serve against France or its allies, nor against His Majesty King Joseph Napoleon, before a year and a day, whether on the continent or in the islands. It is granted 8 field pieces, but the rest of the field artillery, the fortress artillery, and all the magazines of victuals, munitions and other military objects shall be faithfully handed over to the French army without the least thing being removed. It is granted ten days' victuals' (p. 420); 'this 18 July 1806 at 11 in the evening'; 'translated from the Italian original' (p. 422); 'the French entered Gaëte on the 19th at 4 in the morning; the columns of Generals Donzelot and Valentin entered it by the breaches. There were found 140 cannon, 21 mortars, 3 stone mortars, 7 howitzers, 1,850 muskets, 450 pikes or scythes, 2,225 kilograms of powder and 70,000 cartridges: the few projectiles found were of imperfect calibres. So ended the siege, so often delayed, of one of the strongest places in Europe by its position, after 5 months of blockade, 4 of open trench and 11 days of continuous fire' (p. 248); 'the garrison obtained the honours of war and embarked to be taken to Palermo: several of the officers and soldiers took service in King Joseph's troops' (OCR); Colletta, 'Gaeta surrendered on the 18th of the same July' (p. 28); 'although the assaults were prepared for the morning of the 20th, the French, at the first light of the 18th, having formed their troops in column, simulated the movement that in the field usually precedes the moment of mounting the breach'; 'it was agreed that same day to give Gaeta up to the French and to embark the garrison for Sicily, first swearing not to fight against France and its confederates for a year and a day' (p. 30).

claims.value: Bodart places Gaëta, a town in central Italy, Campania, on the Mediterranean, 75 km northwest of Naples. claims.value: Side A lacked a siege train and was short of means for months. Koch: the army of Naples had no siege park and its means were scattered in a kingdom Joseph wished to spare; the engineers estimated the siege at 15 or 20 days and asked for at least 4,000 men, 50 guns and some small armed vessels, and the artillery for 330 milliers of powder and 150,000 infantry cartridges; the fascine and gabion workshops had to be set up in the woods of Fondi, which needed carts that were entirely lacking (OCR). After Joseph became king there were before the place only 23 twenty-four-pounders, 16 twelve-pounders and 8 mortars, with two-thirds of their supply; the powder was mediocre and partly damaged; there were only 4,500 to 6,000 gabions, 9 to 10,000 fascines and 30,000 sandbags; the weak siege corps could not furnish the workers, guards and detachments, infantry companies had to be attached to the artillery, scarcely 500 workers a day could be had, and subsistence often failed; in April and May the workers numbered 100 to 200. On 18 May there were 32 heavy pieces, 16 mortars, 20,000 round shot, 4,800 bombs, 96,000 kilograms of powder and 38,500 infantry cartridges, and the three generals asked for a reinforcement of 3,000 infantry; new negotiations were opened with the Pope for powder (OCR). Before the fire opened on 7 July the pieces were to be supplied with 300 rounds per 24-pounder, 400 per 16-pounder, 150 bombs per 12-inch mortar and 300 per 8- and 9-inch mortar; during the fire General Dedon reported that few resources remained and that many carriages and pieces were in bad state (OCR). The siege consumed 250,000 kilograms of powder, including 380,000 cartridges issued to the troops, and the defence nearly double; 68,700 rounds were fired from the attacks and more than 100,000 from the place; the trenches and batteries used 171,000 sandbags, 9,000 gabions, 32,000 fascines or saucissons and all the barrels, doors and planks of the faubourg, and the money spent came to 430,000 francs. Side B was supplied by sea, by the court of Palermo and the English squadron (claim koch-side-b); deserters said during the fire that the place lacked food (OCR); the French found in it 2,225 kilograms of powder, 70,000 cartridges and a few projectiles of imperfect calibres. Colletta: in the fortress provisions of war and food abounded (OCR); the besiegers brought fascines and gabions from the wood of Fondi, twelve miles from the camp; the fortress fired a hundred thousand balls or bombs in the whole siege, and the other side forty thousand.
claims.rationale: Means and supply as the passages read give them (page images except the passages marked OCR). No supply return was inspected. Koch's 68,700 rounds from the attacks against Colletta's forty thousand from the besiegers, and Koch's more than 100,000 from the place against Colletta's hundred thousand, are recorded, not reconciled. Koch's distance of the Fondi workshops is in the OCR only and is not restated. The means were set by the king's and the marshal's decisions and the state of the kingdom, so the claim is tagged unresolved. English renderings (ours): Koch, 'according to the reconnaissance of the place, the engineers estimated the duration of the siege at 15 or 20 days, and asked as a minimum for 4,000 men of troops, 50 pieces and some small armed vessels (an estimate much too low given the nature of the ground through which the approaches had to be driven, the great extent of the front of attack and the great number of pieces to be counter-battered)'; 'the artillery for its part, naming the various calibres of siege pieces, mortars and field pieces, put its needs at 330 milliers of powder and 150,000 infantry cartridges'; as in claim side-a-command for the siege park (p. 203); 'one was obliged to set up the workshops in the woods of Fondi, at a distance of ... (OCR), which required carts, of which there were none at all' (OCR); 'there were still before the place, in position and in the park, only 23 pieces of 24, 16 of 12 and 8 mortars, with two-thirds of their supply. The powder was of mediocre quality and partly damaged; there were still only 4,500 to 6,000 gabions, 9 to 10,000 fascines and 30,000 sandbags: the weakness of the siege corps did not allow it to furnish the workers, the guards and the detachments'; 'but infantry companies had to be attached as auxiliaries to the artillery troops, and scarcely 500 workers a day could be obtained; besides, subsistence was often lacking' (p. 211); 'night of the 6th to the 7th April'; 'the small number of the workers, which is only 100 to 200 at most, the accidents and the difficulty of the ground make this work long and painful' (p. 212); 'nevertheless, in the night of the 1st to the 2nd May'; 'the number of workers varies from 100 to 200' (p. 218); 'there were, in battery and in the park, 32 heavy pieces, 16 mortars, 20,000 round shot, 4,800 bombs, 96,000 kilog. of powder and 38,500 infantry cartridges. The three generals agreed in asking, given the circumstances, for a reinforcement of 3,000 infantry' (p. 223); 'new negotiations were opened with the Pope to obtain powder' (OCR); 'the supply of the pieces is begun, which is to be 300 rounds per piece of 24, 400 per piece of 16, 150 bombs per 12-inch mortar and 300 per 8- and 9-inch mortar' (p. 233); 'General Dedon, from the statement of the siege supplies, informs the marshal of the few resources left to us and the bad state of a great number of carriages and pieces, and insists on the need to reduce the fire of our batteries, for fear that the powder and the bombs may run short' (OCR); 'new deserters ... confirm the news of the gravity of the governor's wound, adding that the place lacks food and its defenders are exhausted' (OCR); 'the siege consumed 250,000 kilograms of powder, including 380,000 cartridges issued to the troops; the defence consumed nearly double. 68,700 rounds of every kind were fired from the attacks, and more than 100,000 from the place'; 'the trenches and the batteries used 171,000 sandbags, 9,000 gabions, 32,000 fascines or saucissons, all the barrels, all the doors and planks of the faubourg; the expenses in money came to 430,000 francs'; as in claim bodart-winner for the matériel found (p. 248); Colletta, as in claims colletta-side-b and gaeta-ground; 'in the whole siege the fortress fired a hundred thousand balls or bombs, and the other side forty thousand' (p. 30).

claims.value: Both sides fought from works. Side B held the fortress: Colletta says that, its old bastions restored and enlarged in the years up to the treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle and amid the fears of war under Ferdinand, it was in 1806 girdled by two walls and further out by a ditch and two covered ways, works not traced by the rules of art; Koch that the place, rebuilt by its engineers since the peace of Aix-la-Chapelle, was far from a masterpiece, that its works were very irregular and badly flanked and its land front had two irregular enceintes preceded by a double covered way, with the Queen's battery dominating the ground of the attacks (OCR), and that when the French batteries were armed it had 103 heavy pieces, 16 mortars and 7 stone mortars in battery. The breaches were made at the citadel, so called, a large tower, and at the bastion of the Breccia. Side A fought from siege works: Koch has trenches opened in the rock and batteries covered by épaulements, the first parallel carried to the sea to stop sorties, and the marshal's order to Lacour to fortify himself on the coast against attempts by sea (OCR); Colletta has the first parallel formed at the end of May and other works raised on the two shores, as the trenches advanced, to keep off enemy ships and any landing behind the camp, so that the French, assailants and assailed, bore the honours and toils of a double war.
claims.rationale: Code both_fortified: side B defended permanent fortifications, and side A fought from its trenches, batteries and shore works against the sorties and the ships (claim posture). The fortress is permanent (inherited); side A's works were built for this siege, the shore works on the marshal's order (OCR), so they are commander_created in part; one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. A coding that counted only the defended position would give B_fortified. The accounts agree on the code, so they are one claim. English renderings (ours): Colletta, 'but in the years that followed up to the treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, and amid the fears of war under the reign of Ferdinand, the ancient bastions restored and enlarged, it was in 1806 girdled by two walls, and further out by a ditch and two covered ways' (p. 28); 'are not traced by the rules of art, which harms or helps the defences according as the besiegers are learned or inexperienced in war'; 'at the end of May, the guns made ready, some batteries raised at Montesecco, the trench opened and the branches extended toward the two seas of the isthmus, the first parallel was formed'; 'the trenches advanced, and at the same time other works rose on the two shores to keep off the enemy ships or the troops that might wish to land behind the camp; so that the French, assailants and assailed, bore the honours and the toils of the double war'; 'at the end of June the works stood on the ditch, directed at the places where breaches were to be opened, which were two: the citadel (so called improperly, a large tower) and the bastion of the breach, whose name recalls the attacks of another siege' (p. 29); Koch, as in claim gaeta-ground for the rock and the épaulements; 'the details into which we have just entered prove that the place was far from a masterpiece of the art, and that the engineers who had rebuilt it since the peace of Aix-la-Chapelle had not drawn from the position all the advantage possible' (p. 202); 'these works are very irregular and flank each other badly'; 'the land front has two irregular enceintes preceded by a double covered way'; 'the Queen's battery. This battery, built halfway up the slope, dominates the whole ground of the attacks' (OCR); as in claim koch-side-b for the place's guns (p. 236); 'in the night of the 3rd to the 4th the first parallel is carried to the sea, both to stop the sorties and to set up batteries nos. 1 and 2 there' (p. 218); as in claim side-a-command for the coast (OCR).

open_questions: Deferred: the rest of Koch's siege journal (pp. 204-247) beyond the registered pages and selected passages, including his account of the first investment by Reynier's troops, where a search of the parent OCR for the generals' names found Grigny's death before the blockade under Lacour, and of Vallongue's mortal wound later in the siege; both lie outside the registered selection and are not cited. The articles of the capitulation after article 2 (pp. 420-422), read in the OCR and cited only for the wounded and sick; the officer-loss table printed with Bodart's entry, not transcribed; Neapolitan, Sicilian and British reports of the defence and Sidney Smith's correspondence, none inspected; Colletta's account of the siege of 1734 in his first book, to which he refers for the works. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: the date of the Capua capitulation, the distance of the Fondi workshops, the guns of the planned bombardment and of the place in March, the council of war's period of further resistance, the hour of the white flags, the regiments of the blockade and of the assault columns, the requests of 18 May beyond p. 223, the fleet of mid-July and the trench lengths and battery count of Koch's reflections.

Most consequential gap: side B's strength. Bodart gives the garrison 4,000 at first and 7,000 at the end; Koch's composition makes fewer than 6,000 before the siege, the deserters about 6,200 in early July and his reflections 7,000; Colletta has about seven thousand on 7 July and three thousand four hundred prisoners at the surrender. The targeted follow-up searched the parent OCR of Koch's chapter on the siege, from the investment to the reflections, for any other statement of the garrison's strength and found none beyond the passages selected; it also checked pièce justificative n° XI, to which Koch refers for his comparison of 3,000 besiegers with 6,000 defenders, and found a note on King Joseph's guard. A Neapolitan or British return of the garrison could narrow the gap.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side A's strength at the end (Bodart 12,000; Koch about twelve thousand, his state of the troops 12,016 and its ceiling of 12,000; Colletta fourteen thousand); its artillery (Bodart 94 guns; Koch 90 pieces with a mobile battery of 6; Colletta eighty heavy guns and mortars); side B's strength (above); the ships on 7 July (Koch 3 ships of the line and 4 frigates; Colletta four ships of the line and six frigates); the losses (French: Bodart about 1,000 with 86 officers, Koch 819 with 29 officers, both by our arithmetic, Colletta eleven hundred; Neapolitan: Bodart about 1,000, Koch about equal to the besiegers' without 152 deserters, Colletta nine hundred); rounds fired (Koch 68,700 from the attacks and more than 100,000 from the place; Colletta forty thousand and a hundred thousand); the parole (Bodart a year; Koch and Colletta a year and a day); side A's commander (Bodart Masséna for the whole siege; Koch Lacour, then Gardanne from 17 May, with the marshal at Castellone only at the end); the successor's name (Koch Hotz, Colletta Storz); why the prince defended (Koch: Lacour's stiffness; Colletta: higher commands and the honour of war); the morning of the 18th (Colletta: a feint by the French; Koch's OCR: white flags while the assault was being prepared).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his 3,000, 12,000 and 7,000 match figures in Koch, and his 171 guns Koch's captured guns by our arithmetic, but the passages read do not show what he used); Koch (the French history of 1850 from Masséna's papers and the war depot, printing the state of the siege troops and the capitulation as pièces justificatives; second-hand for the garrison, whose July strength it takes from deserters); Colletta (the Neapolitan history by a Neapolitan officer, printed in this edition in 1856; the passages read give him no role at Gaeta and name no source). No passage read shows dependence between Koch and Colletta.
